title: The Orthodox way
hookLine: Metropolitan Kallistos Ware explained Orthodoxy to the West with warmth

lines: HE FELT HE HAD COME HOME.
cards: One Saturday in London, a young Englishman raised in the Church of England wanders into an Orthodox church. The service is in a language he can't follow.
Incense, candles, icons on every wall, a choir with no reason to stop. Nobody explains anything. And yet, he wrote later, he felt he had come home.
He became Kallistos Ware: a monk, a teacher at Oxford, and in time a bishop of the Orthodox Church.
He spent his life writing about Orthodoxy for people who had never been inside one, plainly, like a friend showing you around his house. Today's word is one of his book titles.

teach.h: FAITH AS A WAY, NOT A LIST.
teach.b: First, the way, the word that matters in that title.
In Acts, before they're called Christians, the first followers of Jesus are people of the way: Saul goes to Damascus hunting for, in the King James words, "any of this way."

For Ware, faith was less a set of answers to memorize than a road that changes the walker. Orthodox Christians have a bold word for where it leads: theosis, becoming by grace what God is by nature. Second, the heart.
In Orthodox teaching the heart isn't where feelings live.

teach.h: THE HEART: THE CENTER OF THE PERSON.
teach.b: It's the deep center of the whole person, where mind and will and love meet. Proverbs says: "Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life."

teach.h: THE MIND COMES DOWN INTO THE HEART.
teach.b: Ware quoted a Russian bishop, Theophan the Recluse: to pray is to stand before God with the mind in the heart. Not thinking about God from up in the head. Coming down.
Third, the prayer that carries people there, the Jesus Prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me.
Orthodox writers trace it to a blind man outside Jericho who shouted, "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me."
They repeat it slowly, often on a prayer rope of knots, until, they say, the prayer starts to pray itself. Fourth, the tone.
Ware wrote less like a debater than like a host: here is what we do, here is why we love it, come and see.

how: Orthodox Christians pray the Jesus Prayer, often with a knotted prayer rope, and speak of prayer as standing before God with the mind in the heart.

games.q: you're a blind man by the road outside Jericho. you hear that Jesus is passing. the crowd tells you to be quiet. what do you do?
o: stay quiet so you don't cause a scene.
cry out: Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me.
ask someone else to go and speak for you.
games.why: he cries out, louder still. Orthodox Christians hear in his words the root of the Jesus Prayer.

practice: The monks who prayed the Jesus Prayer were called hesychasts, from hesychia, stillness.
Say the word once inside and let your attention sink from behind your eyes to the middle of your chest; when your mind climbs back up, bring it down again.
If you pray, let the Jesus Prayer ride on your breath; if not, rest in the stillness the word names.

wordCard.voice: The Orthodox way. Kallistos Ware's picture of faith as a road walked with the mind in the heart, shown to outsiders like a host.

orig.note: Greek: heart. in Orthodox prayer, the center of the whole person, not only the feelings.
